doc.title: Jerry Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe and Christian Goodwillie, via Zoom, June 30, 2021

chapter: Selling the store and founding Evidence
title: Why he sold the store in 1989
summary: Long hours, family, retail stress, Tower Records and the coming of CDs led him to sell the store after seventeen years.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: You transitioned to starting a record label and I’m wondering if the change in the music scene caused that to happen somewhat. I read something about the distribution of CDs and so forth. Did it make your — was there a time when your record store became untenable?

It didn’t become untenable. What had happened was I started the store in ’72 and I sold it in 1989. So that was seventeen years. I put in a lot of hours. I put in a sixteen hour day and I had two children who were, I was really starting to miss out on, you know, their childhood. And the — so that was an issue. Another issue was retailing in Center City was extremely stressful — with all the great things that happened in the community that developed within the store, parents taking their children there and then the children taking their girlfriends there, or people taking their parents there, people knowing each other. There was a really great sense of community in that store. It was great and believe me I still miss that every day. But retailing in a city like Philadelphia, your brain and your body can only take it for so long, or at least that was the case for me. I wanted to see my kids more, I was tired of driving downtown, up and back every day for all those years, driving the Schuylkill Expressway, horrible. And the other thing that happened is Tower Records had opened up. And they now make documentaries about Tower Records and people go, “Oh for Tower Records, what wonderful memories I have at Tower, it was such a hip place.” I hated Tower Records. I hated the fact that all of a sudden here was this new place that had way more money than me, advertised way more than me, had fancy plastic bags, yellow and red, and you know, shortly after they opened these bags started coming into my store, you know, and customers — you can’t make customers stay loyal to one’s — not if you’re a record buyer you know. I was never loyal to one record store, why would one? Why would I expect anyone to be loyal to my store? And Tower took some sales but that wasn’t what caused me to sell the business. What caused me to © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

sell the business was it was clear that the future was CDs. And my giant inventory would — of albums that I had put together over seventeen years, loaded with cutouts, out of print records, like trying to get my hands on every saleable jazz record there was, was now going to become obsolete. I was going to have to bring in CDs. I was going to have to limit the number of LPs I had. The cost of obtaining CDs was going — and replacing the records I had, was going to cause me to have more money invested in inventory than ever before. So for all these reasons when I had the opportunity to sell my store and it was a good opportunity, I took advantage of it and I sold it.
